checkpoints: A hardcoded, single lock key such as "jobs" makes every worker contend for the exact same resource no matter which job it actually popped off the queue, so N independent workers doing unrelated work collapse to the throughput of one.

The lock key should encode the specific resource being protected, e.g. `jobs:${job.id}`, so workers processing different job ids acquire different keys and run fully in parallel — only a genuine same-job-id conflict, such as a retry racing the original attempt, still contends.

Even after sharding the key, every acquire attempt — including ones that end up refused — still pays the full cost of N parallel SET NX PX round-trips across all nodes plus the validity computation, so granularity fixes parallelism but does not remove per-attempt overhead.

Setting the per-node commandTimeout close to the TTL (e.g. 900ms against a 1000ms TTL) leaves almost no headroom: one slow node can consume nearly the entire TTL just acquiring the lock, pushing computed validity to zero or negative and forcing a wasted re-acquire.

A safe sizing rule keeps commandTimeout to roughly 10% or less of the TTL and keeps the actual critical section — the real work done while holding the lock — to roughly 30% or less of the validity window, rather than letting either crowd the full TTL.

If the protected work genuinely needs more time than that headroom allows, the correct fix is to raise the TTL itself, not to let commandTimeout or an oversized critical section eat into the remaining validity.

Neither lock sharding nor TTL/timeout resizing weakens correctness: acquisition still requires agreement from a quorum of independent nodes for liveness, and every write is still checked against a monotonic fencing token to reject a stale holder — only what is locked and for how long changes, never the safety guarantees.

The fix can be validated with a throughput test comparing the single global key against the sharded per-job-id keys under the same load, confirming throughput now scales with the number of distinct job ids in flight and that no two workers ever simultaneously hold the lock for the same job id under either scheme.
